output:
I set my jaw, tasting the morning air. Six twenty. Ainsley's likely still moving about, but I've got work to do and ore won't haul itself. I tap the table twice before I speak—always have, always will.

"That's ore calling my name," I say, tipping my cap to my household. "I'll be at the outcrop if anyone needs me. Ainsley, I'll look for you come closing time."

The math's simple enough: I pull 5000 sim from pocket, 240 goes to keeping the roof up, and the rest I'll work with. Food can come after I've earned it.

But first—to my post. Walking. Nine ticks to the outcrop. My teacher used to say the ore knows when someone's coming—first shift of the day, it gives up its best. We'll see about that.

The road's quiet this hour. I pass the same stones I've passed for twenty years, and each one looks like it's waiting for me to notice something different about it. I never do.  Still walking. I settle into the rhythm—left boot, right boot, the weight of my tools shifting against my hip. Ezra Okonjo will be at the workshop by now, probably wondering what vein I'll crack open today. Iron's steady work, copper fetches more if you're lucky with the quality. Gold—well, gold's for someone with more patience than I've got, chasing seams that narrow to nothing.

Four more ticks. The outcrop's scent reaches me before I see it—wet stone and sulfur, the smell of usefulness waiting to be born.

I think about my teacher again. I was fifteen. He was already an old man at forty-five, which tells you something about this work. "Bram," he'd say, "the ore owes you nothing. Your sweat buys what it gives." I tap my pocket twice—the old habit—and wait for the ground to rise up to meet me. I stopped. Ainsley's here—should've said my piece proper while I had the chance. But no, I'm standing now, and the ore's not getting any closer.

"Heading out now," I say, tipping my cap. "Mind the shop."

I tap the table twice and start walking again. Walking again. Nine ticks to the outcrop. No use stopping now—I've got words said and a path to finish. I'll let the road do its work and be at my post when the ground rises up to meet me.   I'm back home. The day's half-gone in my mind, and I've made it nowhere. This is what my teacher meant about patience—I never had enough of it, not for walking, not for waiting.

Fine. I'll do this properly. First things first: the ore's not coming to me. I'll walk to it, do my work, earn my keep. No more stopping to tap tables and second-guess. The math's simple: mine the ore, sell what I pull, keep the roof paid before it comes due.

Step by step. No more thinking, just moving. The user seems to want me to continue walking to the outcrop and start mining. The plan says to keep walking, don't stop, until I arrive. Let me just wait for the movement to complete rather than issuing repeated commands.

Walking. Boots on stone, the rhythm of it. I count the ticks in my head—eight now, seven soon. The ore's waiting, and I won't keep it waiting any longer than I must. My hands know the work better than my mouth knows words. Four more. Three. Two. One.

The outcrop rises ahead, gray and patient. I've come home to my real home. I rest my hand on the stone and feel for the seam.
